Steps.Title: Keep at least two emergency access accounts with permanent Global Administrator
Steps.Summary: Cloud-only break-glass accounts can always sign in and administer the tenant, even when every other admin role is eligible.
Steps.Unchecked: No Maester check yet. The Zero Trust Assessment pack checks it (ZTA.21835) once its results can name steps.

Sources.Note: Create two or more cloud-only accounts on the onmicrosoft.com domain, and in PIM give them Global Administrator as a permanent active assignment, not an eligible one.
The plan leaves no permanent active privileged assignments except the emergency access accounts, which keep Global Administrator.

Steps.Title: Exclude emergency access accounts from Conditional Access
Steps.Summary: Emergency access accounts can still sign in when a Conditional Access policy goes wrong.

Sources.Note: Create the accounts, then exclude them, best through one group, from every enforced policy that can block or limit sign-in. Report-only policies need no exclusion.

Steps.Title: Exclude directory sync accounts from Conditional Access
Steps.Summary: The accounts that Microsoft Entra Connect and Cloud Sync use keep syncing when new policies apply.

Sources.Note: With Microsoft Entra Connect or Cloud Sync, exclude the Directory Synchronization Accounts role from policies that target all users.

Steps.Title: Require a compliant device in Conditional Access
Steps.Summary: Sign-ins from devices that Intune does not mark compliant are blocked.
Rollout: Create the policy in report-only mode and review the sign-ins it would block.
Turn it on for a pilot group.
Turn it on for all users, keeping the emergency access accounts excluded.

Sources.Note: The policy doesn't work as intended without an Intune compliance policy. Create one first, have at least one compliant device, and start in report-only.
A device can be marked compliant only once it is registered in Microsoft Entra ID and enrolled in Intune or a supported partner.
Intune's guide sets up compliance policies before device-based Conditional Access, and tests the new policy with a small group first.

Steps.Title: Domain-joined Windows PCs are hybrid joined to Microsoft Entra ID
Steps.Summary: Windows PCs joined to on-premises Active Directory also have a Microsoft Entra device identity that Conditional Access can use.
Rollout: Turn on hybrid join for a pilot group of varied devices first.
Then turn it on for every computer that should be hybrid joined.
Steps.Unchecked: No check yet. Graph lists the devices that are hybrid joined, but not the domain-joined PCs that are not.

Sources.Note: Hybrid join needs Microsoft Entra Connect syncing the computer objects with their device attributes, and the device setting that lets users register devices.
Roll hybrid join out to a pilot group with targeted deployment before the whole organization.

Steps.Title: Require a compliant or hybrid joined device for administrators
Steps.Summary: Accounts in admin roles can sign in only from a device that Intune marks compliant or that is hybrid joined.
Rollout: Create the policy for the admin roles in report-only mode and review the sign-ins it would block.
Turn it on, keeping the emergency access accounts excluded.

Sources.Note: The hybrid joined option works only for devices that are already hybrid joined, and compliance needs Intune policies. Exclude emergency access accounts; start in report-only.

Steps.Title: Require a compliant or hybrid joined device in Conditional Access
Steps.Summary: Sign-ins from devices that are neither compliant in Intune nor hybrid joined are blocked.
Rollout: Create the policy in report-only mode and review the sign-ins it would block.
Turn it on for a pilot group.
Turn it on for all users, keeping the emergency access and directory sync accounts excluded.

Sources.Note: Either signal will do. Compliance needs devices registered and enrolled in Intune; the hybrid option covers only domain-joined Windows PCs that are hybrid joined.
The all-users template excludes the emergency access accounts and, with Connect or Cloud Sync, the directory sync accounts, and starts in report-only.
Organizations not ready to require managed devices for everyone can start with the policy for administrators.

Steps.Title: Windows devices that sign in are registered with Microsoft Entra ID
Steps.Summary: Windows PCs used for Microsoft 365 have a device identity, so their sign-in tokens can be bound to the device.
Steps.Unchecked: Needs sign-in logs. Graph lists registered devices but not the Windows PCs that sign in without one.

Sources.Note: Token protection binds tokens to Windows devices that are joined, hybrid joined or registered. Sign-ins from other devices show up as unbound requests.

Steps.Title: Block access from unknown or unsupported device platforms
Steps.Summary: Sign-ins from device platforms that Conditional Access doesn't recognize are blocked, so platform-based policies can't be sidestepped.
Rollout: Create the policy in report-only mode and review the sign-ins it would block.
Turn it on, keeping the emergency access accounts excluded.

Sources.Note: Platform conditions read the user agent, so use this block alongside other policies. Exclude the emergency access accounts.

Steps.Title: Require token protection for sign-in sessions on Windows
Steps.Summary: Exchange, SharePoint and Teams accept only device-bound sign-in tokens from Windows desktop apps, so a stolen token can't be replayed elsewhere.
Rollout: Create the policy in report-only mode for a pilot group, desktop apps only, for Exchange, SharePoint and Teams.
Review interactive and non-interactive sign-ins for unbound requests over a full working cycle.
Exclude unsupported device types with a device filter, then turn the policy on for users who are ready and widen it.

Sources.Note: Current Windows builds prompt users on unregistered devices to register. Pilot in report-only and look for unbound sign-ins before you enforce. Exclude emergency access accounts.
Pair the policy with one that blocks unknown platforms, so a client can't avoid it by reporting a different platform.
Windows and Apple devices have separate deployment guides, each with its own prerequisites. This step covers Windows.

Steps.Title: Enabled member users are registered for MFA
Steps.Summary: Users already have an MFA method, so policies that ask for MFA or self-remediation don't leave them stuck.
Steps.Unchecked: No Maester check yet. A readiness check that reports the share of users registered for MFA is planned.

Sources.Note: Users need to register for MFA before a risk policy asks them to remediate. Those who haven't stay blocked until an admin steps in.

Steps.Title: Turn on password hash synchronization
Steps.Summary: Microsoft Entra ID holds hashes of synced users' passwords, so leaked credentials can be matched to those users.

Sources.Note: Leaked-credential detection needs password hash sync for synced users, and only leaks found after it is on are matched, so turn it on early.

Steps.Title: Turn on password writeback
Steps.Summary: Password changes made in Microsoft Entra ID, including risk remediation, are written back to on-premises Active Directory.
Steps.Unchecked: Microsoft Graph doesn't report whether password writeback is on.

Sources.Note: Synced users can clear user risk with a secure password change only when password writeback is turned on.

Steps.Title: Remediate the users that ID Protection already rates high risk
Steps.Summary: Existing high-risk users are investigated, then remediated or dismissed, before risk policies start acting on them.

Sources.Note: Investigate and clear the active risks before you turn the risk policies on.
Learn's deployment plan starts by reviewing the users and sign-ins already in the ID Protection reports.

Steps.Title: Mark known networks as trusted named locations
Steps.Summary: ID Protection treats sign-ins from the organization's own networks as less risky, which cuts false positives.

Sources.Note: Some risk detections use trusted locations to cut false positives, so mark office and VPN ranges as trusted before sign-in risk prompts start.

Steps.Title: Require MFA for medium and high sign-in risk in Conditional Access
Steps.Summary: Sign-ins that ID Protection rates medium or high risk need a fresh MFA, which also clears the sign-in risk.
Rollout: Create the policy in report-only mode and review the sign-ins it would affect.
Turn it on for a pilot group.
Turn it on for all users, keeping the emergency access accounts excluded.
Keep it as its own policy, with no user risk condition.

Sources.Note: A user can't register MFA during a risky sign-in, so an unregistered user is blocked instead of prompted. Exclude emergency access accounts and service accounts.
Keep sign-in risk and user risk in separate policies. For medium and high sign-in risk, ask for MFA and reauthentication every time.
Start sign-in risk policies with a subset of users before the whole organization.

Steps.Title: Require risk remediation for high user risk in Conditional Access
Steps.Summary: Users that ID Protection rates high risk must remediate, with a secure password change or a fresh sign-in, before they get access.
Rollout: Create the policy in report-only mode and review its impact, including the risk-based policy impact workbook.
Turn it on for a pilot group.
Turn it on for all users, keeping the emergency access accounts excluded.
Keep it as its own policy, with no sign-in risk condition.
Steps.Unchecked: MT.1013 accepts only Require password change, not the Require risk remediation control that Learn now recommends, so it can't verify the step yet.

Sources.Note: The policy targets all users and resources, excludes emergency access accounts and service accounts, asks for risk remediation at high user risk, and starts in report-only.
Users not registered for MFA can't self-remediate and stay blocked, and synced users also need password writeback. Clear existing risk before turning the policy on.
Sign-in risk left unremediated raises user risk. A sign-in risk policy lets users clear it with MFA first.
Leaked credentials set user risk to high, and for synced users the detection needs password hash sync.

Steps.Title: Enable passkeys (FIDO2) in the Authentication methods policy
Steps.Summary: Users in scope can register a passkey on a security key, in Microsoft Authenticator or with a passkey provider.
Rollout: Enable it for a pilot group that includes admins, and watch registrations in the Authentication methods activity report.
Give admins a passkey profile that allows only device-bound passkeys.
Widen the targets group by group.

Sources.Note: Turn on Passkey (FIDO2) for the users who will register and allow self-service setup, or they can't add a passkey in Security info.

Steps.Title: Enable Temporary Access Pass
Steps.Summary: Admins can issue a time-limited pass, so a user with no MFA method can sign in and register a passwordless one.

Sources.Note: A pass works only for users in scope of the Temporary Access Pass method, so enable it and target the users who onboard or recover with it.

Steps.Title: Configure Microsoft Entra certificate-based authentication
Steps.Summary: Users can sign in with a smart card or certificate that Microsoft Entra ID accepts as multifactor.
Steps.Unchecked: No Maester or Zero Trust Assessment check yet.

Sources.Note: Certificate-based authentication takes more setup than passkeys, so Learn suggests it only where it is needed.
Only multifactor certificate-based authentication is part of the phishing-resistant strength.

Steps.Title: Administrators have a phishing-resistant method registered
Steps.Summary: Every account that holds an admin role can already sign in with a passkey, Windows Hello for Business, Platform SSO or a certificate.
Steps.Unchecked: No Maester check yet. The Zero Trust Assessment pack checks it (ZTA.21782) once its results can name steps.

Sources.Note: A strength can be met only with methods the tenant has enabled and the user has registered. Any method in the phishing-resistant strength will do.
Admins register a phishing-resistant method before the policy is on, using a Temporary Access Pass if they have no MFA method yet.

Steps.Title: Require phishing-resistant MFA for administrator roles
Steps.Summary: Accounts in admin roles must sign in with a phishing-resistant method to reach any resource.
Rollout: Create the policy for the admin roles in report-only mode and review the sign-ins it would block.
Turn it on for admins on Windows and iOS first, then macOS and Android.
Keep the emergency access accounts excluded.

Sources.Note: Admins without a phishing-resistant method are locked out when the policy turns on, which can lock you out of the tenant. Exclude the emergency access accounts.

Steps.Title: Users have a phishing-resistant method registered
Steps.Summary: Users can already sign in with a passkey, Windows Hello for Business, Platform SSO or a certificate on the devices they use.
Steps.Unchecked: No Maester check yet. A readiness check is planned, and the Zero Trust Assessment pack checks it (ZTA.21801) once its results can name steps.

Sources.Note: Users register a portable credential first and device-bound ones after. New users and users with no MFA method start with a Temporary Access Pass.
A strength can be met only with methods the tenant has enabled and the user has registered. Any method in the phishing-resistant strength will do.

Steps.Title: Require phishing-resistant MFA for all users
Steps.Summary: Every user must sign in with a phishing-resistant method to reach any resource.
Rollout: Create the all-users policy in report-only mode early, before registration campaigns, to see which sign-ins it would block.
Enforce it in waves, one policy per device platform, for groups of users who are ready.
Once almost every user is in a ready group, turn the all-users policy on and remove the per-platform policies.

Sources.Note: A user who hasn't registered a method the strength accepts can't reach the resource, so get users registered before you enforce it.
Enforcement typically starts with admins and then reaches other users in waves by device platform, with the emergency access accounts excluded.
With Connect or Cloud Sync, exclude the Directory Synchronization Accounts role from all-user authentication strength policies.

Steps.Title: Require approval to activate Global Administrator in PIM
Steps.Summary: Each Global Administrator activation waits for a named approver before it takes effect.
Rollout: Name at least two approvers before you require approval.

Sources.Note: With approval on, no named approver and no active Global or Privileged Role Administrator, nobody can approve. Permanent emergency access accounts avoid that lock-out.
The plan's example settings have another Global Administrator approve each Global Administrator activation.

Steps.Title: Send PIM notifications for privileged roles to a monitored mailbox
Steps.Summary: Assignments to and activations of highly privileged roles email a security mailbox as well as the default recipients.

Sources.Note: Each role's PIM settings can copy assignment and activation emails to extra recipients, such as a mailbox the security team watches.

Steps.Title: Make privileged role assignments eligible in PIM
Steps.Summary: Administrators hold privileged roles as eligible assignments they activate when needed. Only the emergency access accounts stay permanently active.
Rollout: Pilot with a small group of admins, and check that activation, approval and notifications work as planned.
Make Global Administrator and Security Administrator assignments eligible first, then the other privileged roles.
Remove service principals from privileged roles or give them time-bound active assignments, since they can't be eligible.
If activation fails in production, make the affected assignments active again, then fix the settings.

Sources.Note: For Microsoft Entra roles, configure the role settings first, then give eligible assignments, then let users activate them just in time.
If every Global and Privileged Role Administrator is eligible and activation needs an approver nobody can be, the tenant is locked out. Keep emergency accounts active.
Pilot with test users, convert the most privileged roles first, and roll back by making assignments active again if activation fails.
